svg.text: WiPhone "woods" backplate — RFM95W + GPS + 915 MHz whip + expanded battery
Rev 2026-08-11. Pin names from Hardware.h (RFM95_CS 27, RFM95_INT 38) + the official WiPhone daughterboard pinout. GPS moved to 3.3 V and the power section rewritten — see the purple band.
Pogo header / screw terminals
SIGNALS (all 3.3 V logic)
GPIO_12 DB_SPI_MISO
GPIO_13 DB_SPI_MOSI
GPIO_14 DB_SPI_CLK
GPIO_27 DB_SPI_CS
GPIO_38 DB_RXD input-only
GPIO_32 DB_TXD
POWER
VBAT 3.4–4.2 V, 1 A fuse
5V VBUS node — 0 V unless USB or pack
GND
D0–D5 + I2C also broken out; unused here.
RFM95W (SX1276, 915 MHz)
GND (both pads)
MISO
MOSI
SCK
NSS ← GPIO_27
RESET leave NC (RFM95_RST = -1)
DIO0 LEAVE UNCONNECTED — frees GPIO_38
mesh_phy.cpp polls; it never attaches an ISR. If the
PHY ever becomes interrupt-driven, this plate breaks.
Antenna chain
ANA → u.FL jack → pigtail
→ SMA bulkhead → 915 whip
The RFM95W has NO u.FL on the module —
only the bare ANA pad. Solder a u.FL jack to
ANA + adjacent GND, or the pigtail direct.
ANA→connector under ~5 mm, 50 Ω,
grounded both sides.
Never key up with no antenna fitted.
HGLRC M100 Mini GPS
V+ ← 3.3 V (module takes 3.3–5 V)
GND
TX → GPIO_38 (ESP32 RX)
RX ← GPIO_32 (ESP32 TX)
Run it from the plate's 3.3 V, not the header's 5 V.
The 5 V pin is dead without USB or the pack, so hanging the
GPS on it would tie your navigation to the battery board.
u-blox M10, UBX/NMEA. Confirm baud on the bench.
Extra parts
1 × u.FL / IPEX MHF jack
1 × u.FL → SMA bulkhead pigtail
1 × 915 MHz SMA whip
1 × 3.3 V LDO/buck (≥250 mA)
2 × 100 nF (RFM 3V3, GPS 3V3)
1 × 10 µF (RFM 3V3 bulk)
1 × 22–47 µF (GPS 3V3 bulk)
1 × polyfuse + connector
optional 10 kΩ pull-up on RESET
No level shifters needed — ESP32, RFM95W
and the GPS UART are all 3.3 V logic.
Backplate 3.3 V rail — give the radio and GPS their own regulator
VBAT → LDO / buck → 3.3 V rail (size for ≥ 250 mA)
EN ← the phone's 3.3V pin
Gating EN on the phone's own 3V3 stops this rail back-powering the
ESP32 through its GPIO clamp diodes when the phone is off.
Don't hang both loads on the phone's MIC5219:
RFM95W TX 120 mA + GPS ~30 mA ≈ 150 mA — at that LDO's 150–200 mA limit.
Extended battery — feed the 5 V pogo pin, exactly like the official Mega pack does
✅ The 5 V pogo pin IS an input — the tap is BEHIND the diode
WiPhone's Mega Battery Pack "acts exactly like an external power bank, but you
don't need a cable since it's connected through the daughterboard headers." Its
IP5306 makes a 5 V 2.4 A boost, and the 5 V pin is the only header pin that can
take it. So the pogo tap sits DOWNSTREAM of the protection, on the charger's side:
USB ─[1 A fuse]─[rev-prot diode]─[limiter]─┬─→ 5 V pogo pin
└─→ charger IC
Every documented fact fits: DRAWING current out crosses the fuse/diode/limiter (hence
"<100 mA" and "drops below 4 V"), it reads 0 V on battery, and PUSHING current in
bypasses all three and goes straight to the charger — which is how the Mega does 2.4 A.
✅ Your question, answered — it is safe, and the diode is why
"What happens when I plug USB in while the pack drives 5 V?"
The Mac's VBUS reaches the node only after the fuse, diode and limiter — call it
~4.6–4.7 V. Your pack sits on the node at 5.0–5.2 V. The pack simply wins: the
diode is reverse-biased, so no current can flow back into the Mac's port — which
is exactly the job that diode was put there to do. D+/D− are untouched, so serial
and flashing behave normally. If the pack sags below ~4.6 V the Mac quietly takes
over. Neither case is a fault.
So the behaviour you want is what the hardware already does.
Cosmetic only: GPIO 37 reads "USB present" whenever the pack is on, so the charge icon blinks.
How to build it
A ✅ RECOMMENDED — copy the Mega: IP5306 module, boost output → the header's 5 V pin
An IP5306 module is the same SoC the Mega uses and is a one-part answer to "mini charging circuit + tiny 5 V booster with its own USB-in": 2.1 A charger,
5 V 2.4 A boost, its own Micro-B in, USB-A out, 4 charge LEDs, key ON/OFF. Add the IP3005A-class protection the Mega pairs with it, plus a fuse in the leg.
The phone's charger then manages the internal cell normally. No cell paralleling, no matched-voltage ritual, hot-pluggable — and it leaves the USB port free.
⚠ IP5306 no-load shutdown: most modules cut the boost when the load drops under ~45–100 mA. If the phone ever idles below that, the pack drops out
mid-use. Check the variant before committing — some expose it as a register/strap setting, and a small bleed resistor is the crude fallback.
⚠ Not documented: whether the phone's own USB can charge the PACK (pass-through). That needs the IP5306's VIN on the same node. Test, don't assume.
B ⚠ Fallback if the 5 V route disappoints — buck/boost to a current-limited ~4.15 V CV → the VBAT pin
Safe *because* it is voltage- and current-limited, which is the exact thing raw paralleling lacks. But it bypasses the phone's charger and confuses the CW2015 gauge.
C 🛑 Hard-parallel the pack onto VBAT — the July 2026 failure that destroyed both packs' protection FETs. No.
⚑ Bench-check first, with the plate off: no USB attached, feed the 5 V pin from a supply at 5 V / 200 mA limit and watch for charging current. That confirms the tap point in a minute.
